introduction: These readings, nearly all from ‘Abdu’l-Bahá's talks, follow a single atom on its travels. The elements of the earth are taken up into the plant, the plant into the animal, the animal into the human body, and each particle passes in the course of ages through every form; nothing is lost, every decomposition is a promotion, and the purpose of the journey is the appearance of human perfections. The passages apply this to diet and to the killing of animals, and cite older philosophers on atoms in motion. All thirty-three quotations are read here beside thirty-three from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: Heraclitus on flux, Plato and Aristotle on the elements changing into one another, Lucretius, Genesis and Ecclesiastes on dust, Rumi's 'I died as mineral', Hamlet's worm and king, Emerson, Whitman and Darwin's 'endless forms'. Five push back or add a side: Bentham asking whether animals can suffer, Tennyson's nature red in tooth and claw and Whitman's contented animals beside the claim that an animal's felicity is to enter the human realm, Darwin telling the ascent without a purpose, and the Gita on the soul changing bodies, which the readings do not teach.
questions: Trace one atom, as the readings do, from soil to a human body. What does the exercise change in how you see your own body?
The readings say a thing destroyed is 'promoted into a world greater than the world it knew'. In what sense, and for whom?
An animal's felicity is said to lie in passing into the human realm. How does that sit with Bentham's question and with Tennyson's line?
Darwin and Lucretius tell a similar story without purpose. What do the readings add with the words 'so that'?
The Gita speaks of a soul taking new bodies; these readings speak only of atoms. Why does ‘Abdu’l-Bahá keep the two apart?

outside.why: Heraclitus said that upon those who step into the same rivers, different and ever different waters flow.
Whitman begins his song by saying that every atom belonging to him as good belongs to you.
Tennyson plucks a flower from a wall and says that to understand it, root and all, would be to know what God and man is.
Rumi tells the same ascent as his own story: I died as mineral and became a plant, I died as plant and rose to animal.
Emerson put it in a couplet: striving to be man, the worm mounts through all the spires of form.
Thoreau asks whether he should not have intelligence with the earth, being partly leaves and vegetable mould himself.
Lucretius founded his account of nature on one rule: nothing from nothing ever yet was born.
Plato's Timaeus observes the elements passing into one another: water becomes stone and earth, and again passes into vapour and air.
Aristotle too holds that the elements change into one another, and asks what persists through the change.
Genesis traces the same path in a sentence: dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.
Marcus Aurelius says that death is such as generation is, a mystery of nature.
Leibniz held that each simple substance has relations which express all the others, and is a perpetual living mirror of the universe.
Ecclesiastes says that all go unto one place: all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again.
Whitman says that for him the nebula cohered to an orb, the long slow strata piled, and vast vegetables gave sustenance.
Pope pictured nature as a chain: strike a tenth or a ten-thousandth link, and you break the chain alike.
Hamlet makes the same point: a man may fish with the worm that hath eat of a king, and eat of the fish that fed on it.
Bentham said the question about animals is not whether they can reason or talk, but whether they can suffer. Does the argument from the progress of matter answer that?
Tennyson set faith in love as creation's law against nature, red in tooth and claw. Is being eaten the animal's felicity, or the cost that the scheme asks of it?
Whitman thought he could turn and live with animals, so placid and self-contained. Do animals need to become something else to have their good?
Jesus said that a corn of wheat abides alone unless it fall into the ground and die, but if it die it brings forth much fruit.
Darwin concluded that man still bears in his bodily frame the indelible stamp of his lowly origin. He tells the ascent without a 'so that'; does purpose belong in the account?
Coleridge sensed one life within us and abroad, which meets all motion and becomes its soul.
Darwin found grandeur in the view that from so simple a beginning endless forms have been, and are being, evolved.
Marcus Aurelius reminds himself that all things from eternity are of like forms and come round in a circle.
Heraclitus said that the way up and the way down are one and the same.
Heraclitus called the world an ever-living fire, kindled in measures and going out in measures.
Shelley wrote that man's yesterday may never be like his morrow: nought may endure but mutability.
The Buddha taught that decay is inherent in all component things, and urged: work out your salvation with diligence.
The Gita says the spirit puts on new bodies as a man puts on new robes. The readings send atoms through the kingdoms, not a soul through lives: what turns on the difference?
Marcus Aurelius advises regarding the universe as one living being, with one substance and one soul.
Wordsworth felt a motion and a spirit that impels all thinking things and rolls through all things.
Tennyson asks man to move upward, working out the beast, and let the ape and tiger die.
Whitman calls himself an acme of things accomplished, and an encloser of things to be.
